Funny thing about “lower premiums”…

Washington always promises savings right before a deadline it helped create.

Here’s what never gets mentioned.

• H.R. 6703 doesn’t replace the ACA it layers parallel insurance markets on top of it, expanding association health plans and HRAs that are exempt from many ACA consumer protections.

• Those plans are cheaper largely because they can exclude higher risk enrollees, limit benefits, or cap coverage, pushing sicker and older Americans back into the ACA pool where premiums rise.

• The bill’s projected savings rely on cost sharing payments flowing directly to insurers, not families stabilizing balance sheets without guaranteeing lower out of pocket costs at the pharmacy or doctor’s office.

• CBO premium “reductions” are averages meaning gains accrue mostly to healthier, employer adjacent workers, while millions in the individual market face higher premiums once enhanced subsidies expire.

• And insurers backing these reforms gain greater pricing flexibility and risk segmentation, the same dynamics regulators warned about when “skinny plans” expanded pre-2018.

So yes, market competition matters.

And yes, ACA subsidies were built on temporary scaffolding.

But shifting risk instead of fixing the structure doesn’t lower health care costs it redistributes them, quietly deciding who pays more and who pays less.

If Congress wanted true premium stability, the long term fix would’ve passed years ago not rolled out as a talking point once the clock started ticking.

And now you know… the rest of the story.
